# Matrix {#sec-matrixCoding}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Tableau matematika!
:::

A matrix is a programming implementation of a mathematical matrix @sec-matrixMath. It is a rectangular object where each element is identified by its row and column position.

Reusing the analogy of a vector as a stacked apartment building @sec-vector, a matrix allows multiple apartments on each floor. An apartment is then identified by its floor number and its position on that floor. Similar to a vector, a matrix must be homogeneous. A matrix can therefore be described by its data type, such as an integer matrix or a numeric matrix.

In data science, datasets are often heterogeneous, in which case a data frame @sec-dataframe or a list @sec-list is used. In general, a matrix object is best suited for mathematical computation.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

To construct a matrix in R, the syntax `matrix()`{.r} is used.

```r
matrix_name <- matrix(data, nrow = n_rows, ncol = n_cols)
```

The `data` argument takes a vector of length `n_rows * n_cols` so that each value is assigned to all the entry of the matrix. By default, R fills matrices column-by-column.

- The dimensions of a matrix represent the number of rows and columns it contains and can be retrieved with `dim()`{.r}. Alternatively, `nrow()`{.r} and `ncol()`{.r} return the row and column counts individually.

- To access an element in a matrix, square brackets with a comma `[row, column]`{.r} are used: `matrix_name[2, 3]`{.r} returns the entry at the second row and third column. The positional indices must be integers.

- In R, negative indices exclude specific rows or columns. For example, `matrix_name[-2, ]`{.r} excludes the second row, while `matrix_name[, -3]`{.r} excludes the third column from the output.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

Constructing the matrix used in @sec-matrixMath.

```{r}
#| echo: true
mat <-
    matrix(c(6, 3, 0, 1, 3, 1, 10, 0, 0.5, 0, 0, 2),
    nrow = 4,
    ncol = 3)
mat
```
Notice that numerical values are automatically formatted in the console output. When a matrix or vector contains at least one decimal number, R displays all numeric values in that structure with consistent decimal formatting (e.g., 6.0 or 3.0) to preserve alignment across rows and columns.


```{r}
#| echo: true

# Access the entire first row by specifying row index 1 and leaving the column index blank
mat[1, ]

# Access the entire first column by specifying column index 1 and leaving the row index blank
mat[, 1]

# Access the entry at row 3, column 2
mat[3, 2]

# Access elements in columns 1 and 2 of the first row
mat[1, c(1, 2)]

# Access rows 2 and 4 across all columns
mat[c(2, 4), ]

# Access columns 1 and 3 across all rows
mat[, c(1, 3)]

```


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}

- The indexing `[row_index, column_index]`{.r} follows the $a_{i,j}$ notation used in mathematics to denote the entry at row $i$ and column $j$ @sec-matrixMath. Leaving one of the dimension blank means seleection all values along that dimension.

- A matrix is typically used for mathematical operations @sec-matrixOperationMath and @sec-matrixMultiplicationMath.

- Notice that there is no separate chapter on vectors in basic mathematics. This is because, mathematically, a vector is a matrix where either the number of rows or the number of columns is equal to one.

- All elements in a matrix must be of the same data type. If different data types are combined, R automatically converts—or coerces—the entire matrix according to a strict hierarchy: Logical < Integer < Numeric < Character. Values lower in this hierarchy are converted to the higher type across all entries. See examples of coercion in @sec-vector.

- Column and row names can also be assigned to a matrix. However, this is not the most common use of a matrix; a data frame @sec-dataframe is more commonly used for named tabular data.

  ```{r}
  #| echo: true


  # Assign names to rows
  rownames(mat) <- c("Rabe", "Rakoto", "Sanda", "Dora")

  # Assign names to columns
  colnames(mat) <- c("Banana", "Strawberries", "Voatsinefy")

  # Display matrix with dimnames
  mat
  ```
